BME Department of Engineering Geology and Geotechnics · Foundation Engineering · The models are schematic sketches.
Bearing failure below a strip footing

Final state of general shear failure below a strip footing in sand. The footing has settled together with the active wedge and tilted towards the side of the failure. The radial shear zone has slipped along the logarithmic spiral, and the passive wedge has been pushed upwards and outwards along the slip surface, so the ground surface has heaved; on the opposite side a crack has opened. The zones are visible on both cut faces, and the heave runs along the whole strip footing.

Below the pad footing the additional stress decreases rapidly with depth. The coloured shells lie at 80, 60, 40, 20 and 10 % of the net contact pressure. The inner shells stick out furthest from the cut-away quarter, so all of them are visible, and the two cut faces show the whole bulb. The shells were computed with Boussinesq, below a uniformly loaded circle of the same area as the 2 × 2 m footing.

Below the tower there is a variable silty-sandy layer about 10 m thick (horizon A), below it soft, sensitive marine clay down to 40 m (horizon B, its upper part the Pancone clay), and dense sand at the bottom (horizon C). The groundwater is 1–2 m deep. The tower has settled about 3 m on average, and the top of the Pancone has been bent down below it into a dish shape. To the south horizon A is more clayey and the upper sand thinner, so the settlement is larger there. In 1990 the tilt was 5.5°; between 1999 and 2001 soil was extracted from below the north side, which reduced it by about 0.5°.

The auger is 10 m deep, and its flights are full of soil: this soil supports the borehole wall, which is why a CFA pile needs no casing or slurry. The concrete is brought by a hose to the rotary head, and from there it runs down the hollow stem of the auger to the base. The rig is controlled by the operator sitting in the cab.
Excavation with an anchored diaphragm wall

For two basement levels, an 8 m deep excavation in sand and sandy gravel, below the groundwater. The 16 m deep diaphragm wall is keyed into the impermeable clay, so dewatering the excavation does not draw down the groundwater of the surroundings. The wall is held by two rows of ground anchors: the upper row is fixed in the sand, the lower one in the sandy gravel. The two rows diverge and run at least 2.8 m apart everywhere, even below the neighbouring building.

The finished site of the “One site, one semester” case study. Building A stands on pad footings in the sand; because of the peat lens, Building B stands on CFA piles, and its two basement levels were built in an excavation supported by an anchored diaphragm wall. The whole course on a single table.
